# Universal gravitation (`universal_gravitation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs laws_of_motion, keplers_laws; helped by calculus, falling_bodies, astronomical_distances
- Core idea: Every body attracts every other with a force proportional to both masses and falling off with the square of the distance. The force that makes an apple fall is the same that holds the Moon: the Moon is 60 Earth radii away, so it should fall towards the Earth 3600 times more slowly than the apple, about 1.4 mm in a second instead of 4.9 m, and that is exactly how much its path curves away from a straight line. The same law gives Kepler's three laws, the tides, the flattening of the Earth at the poles and the return of comets. A planet is a projectile that keeps falling round the Sun without reaching it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Newton 'discovered gravity' or that the apple hit his head; his step was that the force reaches the Moon and follows one law
  - Thinking there is no gravity in orbit; orbiting is continuous falling
  - Leaving out the inverse square, without which nothing can be calculated
  - Being unable to answer 'what is the cause of the attraction?' (Newton declined to say; that is acceptable)
- History: india: 628 – Brahmagupta writes that the Earth attracts bodies as water flows; a qualitative remark, not a law; europe: 1609 Kepler suggests a solar force; 1645 Boulliau mentions an inverse square; 1679–1680 Hooke proposes it to Newton; 1687 Newton, Principia; 1736–1737 Lapland expedition confirms the flattened Earth; 1759 return of Halley's comet; 1798 Cavendish weighs the Earth; 1846 Neptune found by calculation
- Read:
  - Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687)
  - Richard S. Westfall, Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton (1980)
